German beers.Beck's: Brewed in Bremen since 1873 and sold in green bottles. The key on its label comes from Bremen's coat of arms.
German beers.Paulaner: Founded by Italian monks in Munich in the 1600s, it is among the six breweries allowed to serve beer at Oktoberfest.
German beers.Erdinger: A Bavarian wheat beer specialist whose Weissbier is hugely popular with athletes, who drink its alcohol-free version after races.
German beers.Warsteiner: Brewed in the Sauerland town of Warstein, this Pils has been family-owned since 1753 and is among Germany's biggest premium beers.
German beers.Bitburger: This pilsner is brewed in the Eifel town of Bitburg and is known in Germany for its quick, crisp slogan, Bitte ein Bit.
German beers.Spaten: A Munich brewery that helped popularize the amber Märzen lager, and it is one of the six breweries serving at Oktoberfest.
German beers.Weihenstephaner: This Bavarian abbey brewery claims to be the world's oldest still operating, with brewing records going back to 1040.
German beers.Löwenbräu: Munich's lion brewer, with a roaring lion on its label, takes part in Oktoberfest as one of the city's six breweries.
German beers.Krombacher: One of Germany's biggest beer brands, it promoted rainforest protection via a long-running campaign that funded projects with each crate sold.
German beers.Franziskaner: A Munich wheat beer whose name honors Franciscan monks, rich in banana and clove flavors from its special yeast.
German beers.Hofbräu: The Hofbräuhaus in Munich was a royal brewery founded in 1589, and its beer hall remains a major attraction.
German beers.Heineken: Dutch, from Amsterdam, where Gerard Heineken began brewing in 1864. It is a global giant, but not German.
German beers.Stella Artois: Belgian, from Leuven, and not German despite its popularity. Its name means star, referencing Christmas.
German beers.Carlsberg: Danish. Carlsberg began in Copenhagen in 1847 and named itself for the founder's son Carl.
German beers.Pilsner Urquell: Czech. This beer from Plzeň invented golden pilsner in 1842, although German brewers soon made it their own.
German beers.Grolsch: Dutch, brewed in the Netherlands and recognizable by its flip-top ceramic stoppers on traditional bottles.
German beers.Guinness: Irish stout from Dublin, famous for the nitrogen bubbles that give it a creamy head.
German beers.Peroni: An Italian lager, from Rome, with roots in a small 19th-century brewery in Lombardy.
German beers.Corona: Mexican, not German. Corona Extra is one of the best-selling beers worldwide, usually served with lime.
German beers.Kronenbourg: French. Its 1664 beer is brewed in Alsace, a region that was German at times, but the brand is French.
German beers.Tsingtao: Chinese, but with a German past: it was founded in 1903 by German and British settlers in Qingdao. It is a good trap.
German beers.Efes: Turkish, brewed in Istanbul and named for the ancient city of Ephesus. Efes is the leading beer brand in Turkey.
German beers.Amstel: Dutch, founded in Amsterdam in 1870 and named after the river. Not German despite the lager style.
German beers.Hoegaarden: Belgian, a cloudy wheat beer with coriander and orange peel, unlike Germany's clove and banana weissbier.

Rodents.Squirrel: A rodent that buries thousands of nuts each autumn and forgets many, which accidentally plants trees. Its front teeth never stop growing.
Rodents.Beaver: Beavers build dams and lodges, reshaping whole landscapes. Their orange incisors are iron-rich and keep growing.
Rodents.Capybara: The world's largest rodent, up to about 65 kilograms. It is semi-aquatic and gets along with almost every other animal.
Rodents.Porcupine: A rodent covered in about 30,000 quills in some species. Quills detach easily, but porcupines cannot shoot them.
Rodents.Hamster: Hamsters are rodents, and the name comes from the German for to hoard. They can stuff food into their cheek pouches.
Rodents.Gerbil: A desert rodent. Gerbils are social and dig burrows, and they came into pet shops from Mongolia.
Rodents.Chinchilla: A rodent from the Andes with the densest fur of any land mammal, with about 60 hairs growing from each follicle.
Rodents.Guinea pig: A trap by name: it's neither from Guinea nor a pig, but a South American rodent. Its teeth never stop growing.
Rodents.Chipmunk: A small striped ground squirrel, which is a rodent. Its cheek pouches can hold dozens of seeds at a time.
Rodents.Rat: Rats are rodents known for their intelligence. Rats laugh in ultrasonic chirps when they're tickled.
Rodents.Marmot: A large ground squirrel and rodent. The groundhog, which is famous every February, is a type of marmot.
Rodents.Prairie dog: A rodent, not a dog, named for its barklike call. It builds burrow towns and uses a detailed alarm language.
Rodents.Mouse: The most common rodent. Rodents are defined by a pair of ever-growing incisors in both jaws.
Rodents.Rabbit: A trap: a rabbit looks like a giant rodent, but it's a lagomorph. Rabbits have a second pair of tiny incisors behind the front pair.
Rodents.Hare: Hares are lagomorphs, like rabbits. They have four upper incisors, unlike the two of rodents.
Rodents.Shrew: A small insect-eating mammal that looks like a mouse but is not a rodent. It has sharp, pointed teeth.
Rodents.Mole: A digging insectivore, not a rodent. Its powerful, spade-like forelimbs are made for tunnelling.
Rodents.Hedgehog: A spiny insectivore, so not a rodent, even though it is small and furry. It has insect-eating teeth instead.
Rodents.Ferret: A carnivore in the weasel family, not a rodent. Ferrets have been domesticated for centuries to hunt rabbits.
Rodents.Weasel: A slender carnivore that can chase prey into burrows. It is not a rodent, though it hunts them.
Rodents.Bat: The second biggest order of mammals after rodents is bats. They are not rodents, and they can fly.
Rodents.Opossum: A marsupial, not a rodent, although it's rat-sized. Opossums have 50 teeth, more than any other North American land mammal.
Rodents.Pika: A small mountain mammal that looks like a rodent but is a close relative of rabbits. It stores hay for winter.
Rodents.Mongoose: A small carnivore, famous for fighting cobras. It is not a rodent, but it is quick enough to dodge snake strikes.

Dog breeds.Beagle: Beagles have hundreds of millions of scent receptors, which is why they're used to sniff out contraband at airports.
Dog breeds.Poodle: Poodles began as German water retrievers, and the fancy clip was meant to help them swim while protecting their joints.
Dog breeds.Dachshund: Dachshund means 'badger dog' in German, because these long-bodied hounds were bred to dive into badger dens.
Dog breeds.Corgi: The Pembroke Welsh Corgi was Queen Elizabeth II's favorite breed, and she owned more than thirty during her reign.
Dog breeds.Labrador: Despite the name, Labradors come from Newfoundland, not Labrador, and are now popular as guide and detection dogs.
Dog breeds.Husky: Siberian Huskies were bred by the Chukchi people to pull light sleds over long distances, and some have one blue eye and one brown.
Dog breeds.Pug: Pugs trace back to ancient China, where emperors kept them as companions, and their flat faces make heat a real risk.
Dog breeds.Chihuahua: Named after a Mexican state, the Chihuahua is the world's smallest dog breed, often weighing under 3 kilos.
Dog breeds.Dalmatian: Dalmatian puppies are born pure white, and the spots appear within a few weeks.
Dog breeds.Boxer: Boxers probably got their name from the way they bat with their front paws while playing, as if sparring.
Dog breeds.Greyhound: Greyhounds can reach about 70 km/h, the top speed among dogs, yet they are famously happy to nap most of the day.
Dog breeds.Shih Tzu: Shih Tzu means 'lion' in Chinese, and the breed was treasured in Chinese imperial courts as a small lap companion.
Dog breeds.Basenji: Basenjis from central Africa rarely bark and make a yodel-like sound called a 'baroo' instead.
Dog breeds.Siamese: Trap: Siamese is a cat breed, with blue eyes and darker 'points', named for Siam, now Thailand.
Dog breeds.Persian: Trap: Persians are among the oldest cat breeds, and their flat faces can cause breathing and tear-duct problems.
Dog breeds.Maine Coon: Trap: Maine Coons are among the largest domestic cats and are the official cat of the state of Maine.
Dog breeds.Ragdoll: Trap: Ragdoll cats are named for tending to go limp when picked up, and they're cats, not dogs.
Dog breeds.Sphynx: Trap: Sphynx cats look hairless but wear a fine down, and their skin needs regular baths as oil builds up.
Dog breeds.Abyssinian: Trap: Abyssinians are slender cats with ticked coats; despite the name, their true origin is uncertain.
Dog breeds.Clydesdale: Trap: Clydesdales are Scottish draft horses with feathered feet, made famous by a beer brand's wagon team.
Dog breeds.Appaloosa: Trap: Appaloosas are spotted horses, and the Nez Perce people of the Pacific Northwest famously bred them.
Dog breeds.Angus: Trap: Angus are black cattle from Scotland, prized for well-marbled beef, not a dog breed.
Dog breeds.Merino: Trap: Merinos are sheep prized for exceptionally fine, soft wool, now popular for outdoor clothing.
Dog breeds.Holstein: Trap: Holsteins are the black-and-white dairy cows that top the world in milk production.

Herbivores.Giraffe: Giraffes browse treetops with a tongue about 45 cm long. It's tough and dark, which shields it from sunburn and thorns.
Herbivores.Elephant: The elephant is the largest living land animal and eats up to about 150 kg of plants a day. Its trunk holds tens of thousands of muscle bundles.
Herbivores.Cow: Cows spend roughly eight hours a day chewing cud, and have four stomach compartments. Their gut microbes ferment tough grass.
Herbivores.Horse: Horses can sleep standing up, thanks to a locking mechanism in their legs. Their teeth keep growing for most of their lives.
Herbivores.Rabbit: Rabbits eat grass, hay and leafy greens, and yes, their diet should be more hay than carrots. Carrots are sugary treats for them.
Herbivores.Koala: Koalas eat eucalyptus, a diet so low in energy that they sleep most of the day. It's toxic to most other mammals.
Herbivores.Manatee: The manatee is a gentle sea cow that grazes on seagrass. Sailors may have mistaken them for mermaids.
Herbivores.Zebra: Zebras graze mainly on grass. No two have the same stripe pattern, and the stripes may help deter biting flies.
Herbivores.Beaver: Beavers eat bark, leaves and water plants, not fish. They store branches underwater near their lodge as a winter food pantry.
Herbivores.Capybara: The capybara is the world's largest rodent, and an enthusiastic grass eater. It's at ease in water and is often seen with birds on its back.
Herbivores.Kangaroo: Kangaroos eat grasses and shrubs, and their stomach hosts microbes that produce less methane than cows' do. They can't walk backwards.
Herbivores.Bison: Bison are huge grass eaters that once numbered tens of millions across North America. Hunting reduced them to a few hundred by 1900.
Herbivores.Bear: Bears are omnivores, eating berries, roots, fish and even carrion. Polar bears are the exception, being mainly meat-eaters.
Herbivores.Pig: Pigs eat both plants and meat. They're highly intelligent animals and are often said to rank above dogs in some tests.
Herbivores.Raccoon: Raccoons are omnivores that will eat fruit, eggs, crayfish and city leftovers. Their dexterous hands are very sensitive to touch.
Herbivores.Chimpanzee: Chimpanzees mainly eat fruit but also hunt monkeys and use tools to fish termites. That makes them omnivores, not herbivores.
Herbivores.Crow: Crows eat seeds, insects, carrion and scraps, so they're omnivores. They can recognise individual human faces and hold grudges.
Herbivores.Rat: Rats eat almost anything, from grain to meat, making them omnivores. They can also laugh when tickled, in ultrasonic squeaks.
Herbivores.Chicken: Chickens eat seeds, but also insects, worms and even small mice. They are descended from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia.
Herbivores.Fox: Foxes eat rodents, birds, insects and fruit, and are omnivores. A fox can find mice under snow using Earth's magnetic field.
Herbivores.Lion: Lions are strict meat-eaters, hunting large grazers. Females, not males, do most of the hunting.
Herbivores.Crocodile: Crocodiles are carnivores that wait for prey at the water's edge. A saltwater crocodile has the strongest bite measured in any animal.
Herbivores.Badger: Badgers are omnivores, eating earthworms, roots and small animals. A single badger can eat hundreds of earthworms in a night.
Herbivores.Seagull: Seagulls scavenge fish, crabs, rubbish and even other birds' eggs. That omnivorous habit is why they thrive in towns.

Cities in Spain.Madrid: Madrid sits at about 650 meters, making it one of Europe's highest big capitals, and its Prado holds Velázquez and Goya masterpieces.
Cities in Spain.Barcelona: Barcelona's Sagrada Família has been under construction since 1882, and Gaudí's towering basilica is still not completely finished.
Cities in Spain.Seville: Seville is the home of flamenco and the original setting of the opera The Barber of Seville, and its orange trees line the streets.
Cities in Spain.Bilbao: Bilbao was transformed by the Guggenheim Museum in 1997, whose titanium curves are coated in metal like fish scales.
Cities in Spain.Málaga: Málaga is the birthplace of Picasso, and it has a Picasso museum in the old town.
Cities in Spain.Zaragoza: Zaragoza is a city on the Ebro, and has a basilica with a famous pillar that Spaniards believe the Virgin Mary stood upon.
Cities in Spain.San Sebastián: San Sebastián has one of the world's highest numbers of Michelin stars per capita, and is famed for pintxos, snacks on toothpicks.
Cities in Spain.Cádiz: Cádiz is said to be Western Europe's oldest city, founded by Phoenicians about 3,000 years ago.
Cities in Spain.Alicante: Alicante is a Mediterranean port, and where nougat, turrón, is a famous sweet.
Cities in Spain.Marbella: Marbella is a glitzy resort on the Costa del Sol, popular with the international jet set.
Cities in Spain.Benidorm: Benidorm packs one of Europe's densest skylines into a beach resort, with high-rises on a small strip of coast.
Cities in Spain.Lisbon: Lisbon is Portugal's capital, and most of it was rebuilt after a massive earthquake in 1755.
Cities in Spain.Porto: Porto is in Portugal, and gave its name to port wine, aged in cellars along the Douro river.
Cities in Spain.Faro: Faro is a Portuguese city in the Algarve, close to Spain and a popular tourist hub.
Cities in Spain.Coimbra: Coimbra is in Portugal, and has one of Europe's oldest universities, founded in 1290.
Cities in Spain.Buenos Aires: Buenos Aires is Argentina's capital, and the birthplace of the tango.
Cities in Spain.Mexico City: Mexico City is in North America, and was built on the ruins of Aztec Tenochtitlan.
Cities in Spain.Bordeaux: Bordeaux is a French city, and famed for its wine.
Cities in Spain.Marseille: Marseille is France's oldest city, founded by Greeks around 600 BC.
Cities in Spain.Toulouse: Toulouse is France's aircraft capital, where Airbus assembles planes, and is nicknamed the Pink City for its bricks.
Cities in Spain.Naples: Naples is in Italy and is the birthplace of pizza.
Cities in Spain.Montevideo: Montevideo is the capital of Uruguay, and where the 1930 first World Cup was held.
Cities in Spain.Havana: Havana is the capital of Cuba, a city of colorful colonial buildings.
Cities in Spain.Andorra la Vella: Andorra la Vella is the highest capital in Europe at about 1,000 meters, in a tiny country between Spain and France.

Cities in France.Paris: The Eiffel Tower was meant to be temporary, built for the 1889 World's Fair, and it grows by up to 15 cm in summer heat.
Cities in France.Lyon: Lyon is considered France's gastronomic capital, and it is where the Lumière brothers invented cinema.
Cities in France.Marseille: Marseille is France's oldest city, founded by Greek sailors around 600 BC, and it is the home of bouillabaisse.
Cities in France.Nice: Nice was part of Italy until 1860, and its Promenade des Anglais runs along the Riviera.
Cities in France.Bordeaux: Bordeaux has some of the world's most celebrated vineyards, and its city center is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Cities in France.Toulouse: Toulouse is called La Ville Rose for its pink brick, and it is where Airbus builds its planes.
Cities in France.Strasbourg: Strasbourg has swapped between French and German rule, and now houses the European Parliament.
Cities in France.Lille: Lille is a northern city where Charles de Gaulle was born, close to Belgium.
Cities in France.Nantes: Nantes is the birthplace of Jules Verne, and it has a giant mechanical elephant that walks.
Cities in France.Cannes: Cannes hosts a famous film festival every May, where the top prize is the Palme d'Or.
Cities in France.Avignon: Avignon was the papal seat in the 1300s, when popes lived in its enormous palace instead of Rome.
Cities in France.Brussels: Brussels is the capital of Belgium, and the home of the EU's main institutions.
Cities in France.Geneva: Geneva is in Switzerland, and home to the Red Cross and many UN offices.
Cities in France.Lausanne: Lausanne is a Swiss city and the home of the International Olympic Committee.
Cities in France.Monaco: Monaco is an independent city-state on the French coast, not part of France.
Cities in France.Liège: Liège is in Belgium, and is known for waffles and its French-speaking culture.
Cities in France.Quebec City: Quebec City is in Canada, and is mostly French-speaking, but is not in France.
Cities in France.Montreal: Montreal is in Canada, a major French-speaking city on the St. Lawrence.
Cities in France.Antwerp: Antwerp is in Belgium, and a global center of diamond trading.
Cities in France.Luxembourg: Luxembourg City is the capital of the tiny Grand Duchy, a separate country.
Cities in France.Turin: Turin is in Italy, not far from the French border.
Cities in France.Barcelona: Barcelona is in Spain, just south of the French border in Catalonia.
Cities in France.San Sebastián: San Sebastián is in Spain, a few kilometers from the French border.
Cities in France.Andorra la Vella: Andorra la Vella is the capital of Andorra, a tiny country in the Pyrenees, ruled by a French and a Spanish co-prince.

Parts of the eye.Retina: The light-sensing layer at the back of the eye. Its image arrives upside down, and the brain flips it.
Parts of the eye.Cornea: The clear dome at the front has no blood vessels, so it can be transplanted with little rejection risk. It does most of the eye's focusing.
Parts of the eye.Iris: The colored ring controlling pupil size. Its pattern is unique to each person, and even your two eyes differ, which is why it's used for ID scans.
Parts of the eye.Pupil: The black hole in the center of the eye is actually an opening letting light in. It shrinks in bright light and widens in the dark.
Parts of the eye.Lens: A clear flexible disc behind the iris that changes shape to focus. With age it stiffens, which is why many people need reading glasses after 40.
Parts of the eye.Sclera: The white of the eye is tough connective tissue. Humans have an unusually visible sclera, which may help us see where others are looking.
Parts of the eye.Optic nerve: Roughly a million fibers carry signals to the brain. Where it leaves the eye is the blind spot, which has no light-sensing cells.
Parts of the eye.Macula: A tiny central part of the retina responsible for sharp detail, like reading faces. Its decline with age causes macular degeneration.
Parts of the eye.Conjunctiva: A thin, clear membrane covering the white of the eye and lining the lids. It is the part that gets inflamed in pink eye.
Parts of the eye.Vitreous humor: The clear gel filling most of the eyeball, keeping its shape. Floaters you sometimes see are bits of it clumping.
Parts of the eye.Cochlea: A trap: a snail-shaped organ in the inner ear, converting sound to nerve signals.
Parts of the eye.Eardrum: A trap: this thin membrane is part of the ear, not the eye. It vibrates with sound and is only about a centimeter across.
Parts of the eye.Anvil: A trap: the incus is the middle bone of the ear's three tiny bones, named for a blacksmith's anvil.
Parts of the eye.Stirrup: A trap: the stapes is the smallest bone in the body, in the ear, shaped like a riding stirrup.
Parts of the eye.Hammer: A trap: the malleus is a tiny ear bone, shaped like a mallet. It passes eardrum vibrations inward.
Parts of the eye.Uvula: A trap: it's the dangling tissue at the back of the throat, not the eye. It helps keep food from the nose when swallowing.
Parts of the eye.Septum: A trap: the septum divides the nostrils, and the heart also has one. Neither is in the eye.
Parts of the eye.Tonsil: A trap: lymph tissue in the throat, not the eye. It helps catch germs entering by mouth.
Parts of the eye.Alveoli: A trap: tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen enters the blood. You have hundreds of millions.
Parts of the eye.Atrium: A trap: it's an upper chamber of the heart, not part of the eye. The word means entrance hall in Latin.
Parts of the eye.Larynx: A trap: the voice box sits in the throat, not the eye, and holds the vocal cords that produce your voice.
Parts of the eye.Nostril: A trap: part of the nose. Each nostril leads to its own passage, divided by the septum.
Parts of the eye.Molar: A trap: it's a back tooth built for grinding food, nowhere near the eye. Adults usually have twelve, including wisdom teeth.
Parts of the eye.Epiglottis: A trap: a flap of cartilage that closes over the windpipe while you swallow. It's in the throat.

Minerals (not rocks).Quartz: One of the most common minerals in Earth's crust, made of silicon and oxygen. It's used in watches because it vibrates at a steady rate under electricity.
Minerals (not rocks).Feldspar: The most abundant mineral group in the crust, making up around half of it. Its name comes from the German for field spar.
Minerals (not rocks).Mica: A mineral that splits into thin, flexible sheets. It gives makeup its shimmer and was once used as window glass.
Minerals (not rocks).Calcite: Calcite makes up limestone and marble. A clear crystal of it can show a double image, so text seen through it appears twice.
Minerals (not rocks).Halite: Halite is the mineral name for rock salt. It's the table salt we eat, mined or evaporated from seawater.
Minerals (not rocks).Gypsum: A soft mineral you can scratch with a fingernail. It's the main ingredient of plaster and drywall.
Minerals (not rocks).Pyrite: Fool's gold, a brassy mineral made of iron and sulfur. It can spark when struck against steel, and its name comes from the Greek word for fire.
Minerals (not rocks).Talc: The softest mineral on the Mohs scale, rated 1. It's the main ingredient in talcum powder.
Minerals (not rocks).Fluorite: A colorful mineral that gave us the word fluorescence, because many specimens glow under ultraviolet light.
Minerals (not rocks).Magnetite: A naturally magnetic iron oxide. Lodestones, which ancient navigators used as early compasses, are magnetite.
Minerals (not rocks).Hematite: An iron ore that leaves a red-brown streak. Its name comes from the Greek word for blood.
Minerals (not rocks).Galena: The main ore of lead, with silvery, cube-shaped crystals. Early radio sets used it as a crystal detector.
Minerals (not rocks).Olivine: A green mineral that's abundant in Earth's mantle. Its gem form is peridot, and it's been found in meteorites too.
Minerals (not rocks).Granite: A rock, not a mineral, since it's a mix of quartz, feldspar and mica. Its speckled look comes from those separate minerals.
Minerals (not rocks).Basalt: A volcanic rock made of several minerals, and the most common rock on the ocean floor. The Moon's dark plains are basalt too.
Minerals (not rocks).Marble: A rock formed when limestone is transformed by heat and pressure. Michelangelo's David was carved from it.
Minerals (not rocks).Slate: A rock formed from shale by gentle metamorphism, and it splits into flat sheets. It's used for roofs and old school writing tablets.
Minerals (not rocks).Sandstone: A rock made of cemented sand grains, often quartz. Many famous desert canyons and arches are carved from it.
Minerals (not rocks).Limestone: A rock made largely of calcite, and often built from shells and coral. The pyramids of Giza were built mostly from it.
Minerals (not rocks).Obsidian: A volcanic glass formed when lava cools too quickly for crystals to grow. It can be sharper than a surgeon's steel scalpel.
Minerals (not rocks).Pumice: A volcanic rock so full of gas bubbles that it floats on water. Rafts of it can drift across oceans for years.
Minerals (not rocks).Shale: A fine-grained rock that splits into thin layers. It's formed from compacted mud and often holds fossils.
Minerals (not rocks).Coal: A rock made of compressed plant matter, not a mineral, since it's organic. It's formed from swamp forests of 300 million years ago.
Minerals (not rocks).Gneiss: A banded metamorphic rock formed under extreme heat and pressure. Some gneiss from Greenland is nearly 4 billion years old.

Animals with a beak or bill.Parrot: A parrot's beak works like a third foot for climbing, and it is strong enough to crack nuts.
Animals with a beak or bill.Puffin: A puffin's colorful beak is at its brightest in spring and shrinks in winter, and it can hold a dozen small fish at once.
Animals with a beak or bill.Toucan: A toucan's huge beak can be a third of its body length, but it is hollow and light, and helps it cool off.
Animals with a beak or bill.Duck: Ducks' bills have sensitive nerves and comb-like edges that strain food out of water.
Animals with a beak or bill.Eagle: An eagle's hooked beak is built to tear flesh, and its sharp eyesight spots prey from miles away.
Animals with a beak or bill.Octopus: An octopus has a hard parrot-like beak, its only hard part, so it can squeeze through any gap its beak fits.
Animals with a beak or bill.Squid: Squid have a sharp beak in the middle of their arms, and it is the part most often found in sperm whale stomachs.
Animals with a beak or bill.Turtle: Turtles have no teeth and use a beak-like horny edge to bite, even though they are reptiles, not birds.
Animals with a beak or bill.Platypus: The platypus is a mammal with a duck-like bill. It is covered in electroreceptors that find prey underwater.
Animals with a beak or bill.Penguin: Penguins have beaks that are narrow and sharp for catching slippery fish, and are also birds that cannot fly.
Animals with a beak or bill.Pelican: A pelican's bill pouch can hold up to about 10 liters, more than its stomach, and it scoops fish from water.
Animals with a beak or bill.Echidna: The echidna is a spiny egg-laying mammal with a long snout, not a beak, and it has a sticky tongue for ants.
Animals with a beak or bill.Anteater: Anteaters have a long tube-shaped snout, not a beak, and no teeth, and flick their tongue about 150 times a minute.
Animals with a beak or bill.Aardvark: The aardvark has a pig-like snout and a long sticky tongue for termites, but no beak. Its name means 'earth pig'.
Animals with a beak or bill.Swordfish: A swordfish's 'sword' is an extension of the upper jaw and is more of a blade than a beak.
Animals with a beak or bill.Narwhal: A narwhal's tusk is an elongated tooth that can reach about 2.5 meters, so it is a tooth, not a beak.
Animals with a beak or bill.Elephant: An elephant's trunk is a fused nose and upper lip with tens of thousands of muscles, and no beak anywhere.
Animals with a beak or bill.Mosquito: A mosquito has a needle-like proboscis for sipping, which is not a beak, even though it is a pointed mouthpart.
Animals with a beak or bill.Butterfly: Butterflies drink through a coiled proboscis, like a straw, and also taste with their feet. They have no beak.
Animals with a beak or bill.Tapir: A tapir has a short flexible trunk, which is a nose and lip, and no beak, though its babies are born with stripes.
Animals with a beak or bill.Sawfish: A sawfish has a toothy saw-shaped snout, which is not a beak, and it is a ray-like shark relative.
Animals with a beak or bill.Bat: Bats are mammals with snouts and teeth, not beaks, and are the only mammals that truly fly.
Animals with a beak or bill.Shark: Sharks have rows of replaceable teeth, and may use thousands in a lifetime, but nothing like a beak.
Animals with a beak or bill.Hedgehog: A hedgehog has a pointed snout and small teeth, not a beak, and it has about 5,000 spines.

Types of precipitation.Rain: Rain forms when cloud droplets merge until they are heavy enough to fall, and raindrops are not teardrop-shaped, but more like a hamburger bun.
Types of precipitation.Snow: Snow forms when vapor freezes straight into ice crystals, and flakes clump into snowflakes. Their six-armed symmetry comes from water's molecular shape.
Types of precipitation.Sleet: Sleet is rain that freezes on the way down into small ice pellets, and the name is different in the UK, where it means rain mixed with snow.
Types of precipitation.Hail: Hailstones grow in layers as they are tossed up and down in storm clouds, and the heaviest on record weighed about a kilogram, in Bangladesh in 1986.
Types of precipitation.Drizzle: Drizzle is rain with droplets under half a millimeter wide, so small that they seem to float.
Types of precipitation.Freezing rain: Freezing rain falls as liquid but freezes on contact, glazing roads and power lines with ice. It is one of winter's most dangerous kinds.
Types of precipitation.Graupel: Graupel is soft, crumbly pellets formed when snowflakes are coated with freezing droplets, and also called snow pellets.
Types of precipitation.Ice pellets: Ice pellets are small frozen drops that bounce when they hit the ground, and that's what meteorologists call sleet in North America.
Types of precipitation.Snow grains: Snow grains are tiny flat white ice particles, like frozen drizzle, and they do not bounce.
Types of precipitation.Diamond dust: Diamond dust is ice crystals falling from a clear sky in extreme cold, which sparkle in sunlight, and are common in polar regions.
Types of precipitation.Fog: Fog is a cloud touching the ground, floating droplets that do not fall, so it is not precipitation.
Types of precipitation.Dew: Dew forms on surfaces when air cools and moisture condenses, and it never falls from the sky, so it isn't precipitation.
Types of precipitation.Frost: Frost is ice that forms directly on cold surfaces from vapor, and it does not fall from clouds as precipitation.
Types of precipitation.Mist: Mist is a thin fog of floating droplets that hangs in the air without falling, so it is not precipitation.
Types of precipitation.Humidity: Humidity is just the amount of water vapor in the air, invisible and not falling, so it is not precipitation.
Types of precipitation.Clouds: Clouds hold the water that makes precipitation, but until the drops get heavy, they just float.
Types of precipitation.Rainbow: A rainbow is light bent by rain, but it is an optical effect, not the precipitation itself.
Types of precipitation.Wind: Wind moves air around, and has no water falling from the sky, so it is not precipitation, though it drives the rain.
Types of precipitation.Smog: Smog is smoke and fog, or pollution haze, and the word was coined in the early 1900s. It is not falling water.
Types of precipitation.Thunder: Thunder is the sound of lightning heating air, and can be heard about 10 miles away, but it is not precipitation.
Types of precipitation.Lightning: Lightning is electrical discharge. It accompanies storms but is not falling water or ice.
Types of precipitation.Haze: Haze is dust or smoke particles in the air that reduce visibility, not precipitation.
Types of precipitation.Rime: Rime is ice formed when supercooled fog freezes on surfaces, and it is deposited, not falling.
Types of precipitation.Condensation: Condensation is vapor turning into liquid, as on a cold glass, and it is a process, not precipitation.

Visible from Earth with the naked eye.The Moon: The Moon is the only natural object beyond Earth that shows visible surface features to the naked eye, and it's drifting away from us by about 3.8 cm each year.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Venus: Venus is the brightest planet, outshining every star, and can cast shadows in dark skies.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Mars: Mars glows red because of iron oxide on its surface, and shines brightest about every two years, when Earth passes it.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Jupiter: Jupiter is usually the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon and Venus, and its four big moons need only binoculars.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Saturn: Saturn is visible to the naked eye as a steady golden star, but its rings need a telescope to see.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Mercury: Mercury is hard to spot since it stays close to the Sun, so it is only visible low near twilight.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Andromeda Galaxy: The Andromeda Galaxy is the farthest object visible without a telescope, a faint smudge about 2.5 million light-years away.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.ISS: The ISS is the brightest manmade object in the sky, and it can be easy to see as it crosses it in minutes.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Milky Way: From dark sites the Milky Way appears as a band of light, since we are looking along our galaxy's disk from inside.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Orion Nebula: The Orion Nebula is a fuzzy patch in Orion's sword, and is a stellar nursery about 1,300 light-years away.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Pleiades: The Pleiades are a star cluster, the Seven Sisters, and most people see six or seven stars, though it holds hundreds.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Halley's Comet: Halley's Comet is visible to the naked eye as it passes, about once every 76 years, and next returns in 2061.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Polaris: Polaris, the North Star, is not the brightest star as often assumed, but stays almost fixed in the north sky.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Neptune: Neptune is too faint to see without a telescope, and was found in 1846 by mathematical prediction first.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Pluto: Pluto is far too faint, at magnitude about 15, and needs a decent telescope. It was found in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Proxima Centauri: Proxima Centauri is the nearest star after the Sun, yet at 4.2 light-years it is too dim to see without a telescope.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Voyager 1: Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object, over 20 billion km away, and far too faint to see.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Charon: Charon is Pluto's largest moon, half its size, and far too faint and too close to Pluto to see unaided.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Titan: Titan, Saturn's moon, has a thick atmosphere, but it is too faint to see unaided, so you need a telescope.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Black holes: Black holes emit no light, so they can't be seen directly; we infer them from effects on nearby stars.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Eris: Eris is a dwarf planet about as big as Pluto, and its discovery in 2005 triggered Pluto's reclassification, but it is too faint to see unaided.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Triton: Triton is Neptune's large moon, and it orbits backward, but it is too faint to see without a telescope.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Sedna: Sedna is a distant dwarf planet-like object, on a huge orbit lasting about 11,000 years, and invisible without telescopes.
Visible from Earth with the naked eye.Arrokoth: Arrokoth is a snowman-shaped object in the Kuiper belt, visited by New Horizons in 2019, which is too faint to see.

Doctor Who monsters and villains.Cybermen: Cybermen are humans who replace their organs with machinery and suppress emotion. They first appeared in 1966.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Weeping Angels: These statues move only when unobserved. They debuted in 2007's 'Blink', written by Steven Moffat, which became fan-favorite.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.The Master: The Doctor's fellow Time Lord and archnemesis debuted in 1971 with Roger Delgado, and was later reimagined as Missy.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Davros: Davros, the crippled creator of the Daleks, first appeared in 1975's Genesis of the Daleks, written by Terry Nation.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Sontarans: Sontarans are potato-headed clone soldiers bred for endless war. Their weak spot is the probic vent at the back of the neck.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Silurians: The reptilian Silurians come from Earth's ancient past, but their name is a goof, since real Silurian rocks predate reptiles.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Zygons: Zygons are shapeshifters from 1975's Terror of the Zygons, where they kept the Loch Ness Monster as a pet.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.The Silence: The Silence are tall aliens you forget the moment you look away, introduced in 2011 against Matt Smith's Doctor.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Slitheen: The Slitheen are green aliens from Raxacoricofallapatorius who hide in human skin suits and let out gas when they squeeze themselves in.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Klingons: Klingons are Star Trek's warrior aliens, and linguist Marc Okrand built the Klingon language, which has real fluent speakers.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Borg: The Borg, with their 'Resistance is futile', debuted in Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1989, long after the Cybermen.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Romulans: Romulans are Star Trek's Vulcan cousins, named for Rome's founder Romulus, and first appeared in 1966.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Ferengi: The Ferengi are Star Trek's profit-obsessed aliens, and they live by the 285 Rules of Acquisition.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Stormtroopers: Star Wars' Imperial soldiers famously can't aim, and the name echoes the German WWI 'Sturmtruppen' shock troops.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Sith: The Sith are Star Wars's dark-side Force users, bound by the Rule of Two: one master and one apprentice.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Xenomorphs: The Alien creature was designed by Swiss artist H. R. Giger, and its acid blood helps it endure the hull.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Predators: The 1987 Predator suit was redesigned by Stan Winston after the first version looked silly, creating the mandibled face we know.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Decepticons: Decepticons are the evil Transformers, led by Megatron, and the franchise began as a Hasbro toy line in 1984.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Gremlins: Joe Dante's 1984 film Gremlins turned the pilot legend into screen monsters, but they never crossed paths with the Doctor.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Dementors: Dementors belong to Harry Potter, not Doctor Who. They guard Azkaban and are driven away by the Patronus charm.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Orcs: Orcs are Tolkien's creatures, and Doctor Who's closest equivalent might be the Sontarans, who also love battle.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Vogons: Vogons come from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, famed for the third-worst poetry in the universe. Adams also wrote for Doctor Who.
Doctor Who monsters and villains.Replicants: Replicants are the bioengineered humans of Blade Runner (1982). In Philip K. Dick's source novel they're called androids.

Names for groups of performers.Duo: A duo is two performers, and the word comes from Latin for two; the name is used for acts from Simon and Garfunkel to Daft Punk.
Names for groups of performers.Trio: A trio is three performers; in jazz it usually means piano, bass and drums.
Names for groups of performers.Quartet: The string quartet, two violins, a viola and a cello, is regarded as the classical gold standard of chamber music.
Names for groups of performers.Quintet: Quintet means five, and Schubert's 'Trout' Quintet is a famous piece that adds a double bass to the usual strings.
Names for groups of performers.Sextet: A sextet has six performers, and Brahms wrote two famous string sextets, rich-sounding works with two of each of three string instruments.
Names for groups of performers.Septet: Septet means seven performers, and Beethoven's Septet was one of his most popular works during his lifetime.
Names for groups of performers.Octet: An octet has eight players; Mendelssohn wrote his famous string octet at just sixteen.
Names for groups of performers.Nonet: A nonet has nine performers, and it is rarer than the others; Louis Spohr wrote a famous one in 1813.
Names for groups of performers.Duet: Duet is the piece or performance for two, and the word is Italian, from 'duetto'.
Names for groups of performers.Sonnet: Trap: a sonnet has fourteen lines and no performers, so it only looks the part.
Names for groups of performers.Sonata: Trap: a sonata is a piece of music, not a group of musicians.
Names for groups of performers.Minuet: Trap: a minuet is a slow dance, and it ends in -et but has nothing to do with numbers.
Names for groups of performers.Clarinet: Trap: clarinet ends in -et but is a woodwind instrument, not a number of performers.
Names for groups of performers.Cornet: Trap: a cornet is a small brass instrument like a trumpet.
Names for groups of performers.Bassinet: Trap: a bassinet is a baby's bed, with no musical meaning.
Names for groups of performers.Octave: Trap: it sounds like it means eight, and in music it does, but it is an interval, not a performing group.
Names for groups of performers.Octopus: Trap: an octopus has eight arms, but it is an animal, not a group of performers.
Names for groups of performers.Triangle: Trap: a triangle has three sides, and it is also a percussion instrument, but not a trio.
Names for groups of performers.Quarter: Trap: a quarter is one of four parts, but not a group of performers.
Names for groups of performers.Tricycle: Trap: a tricycle has three wheels, not three players.
Names for groups of performers.Trident: Trap: a trident is a three-pronged spear, with no performing meaning.
Names for groups of performers.Pentagon: Trap: a pentagon has five sides, but it is a shape and a famous building, not a quintet.
Names for groups of performers.Spinet: Trap: a spinet is a small harpsichord or piano, not a group.
Names for groups of performers.Castanet: Trap: a castanet is a hand-held clapper used in Spanish dance, and it ends in -et only by chance.

Words that go before 'drum'.Bass: The big bass drum anchors a marching band's beat. In a drum kit it is struck by a foot pedal.
Words that go before 'drum'.Snare: The rattling wires under its head give the snare its crack. Snare drums are staples of military and rock music.
Words that go before 'drum'.Ear: The eardrum is a thin membrane that vibrates with sound. It is only about a centimeter across, but it starts all hearing.
Words that go before 'drum'.Steel: A steel drum is made from an oil barrel, hammered into tuned notes. The instrument was developed in Trinidad.
Words that go before 'drum'.Oil: An oil drum holds about 55 US gallons, while a barrel of crude oil measures 42. The two are not the same.
Words that go before 'drum'.Kettle: Kettledrums, or timpani, are pitched by pedals that tune the head. Orchestras usually have a set of four.
Words that go before 'drum'.Side: A side drum is another name for the snare drum, because it was slung from the player's side.
Words that go before 'drum'.Bongo: A pair of small Cuban drums played with the hands. They're joined by a bridge of wood.
Words that go before 'drum'.Conga: The tall Afro-Cuban drum is played with the hands and is central to salsa. It shares its name with the conga line dance.
Words that go before 'drum'.Talking: Talking drums from West Africa can mimic the tones of speech. Players squeeze cords to change pitch.
Words that go before 'drum'.Hum: Humdrum means dull and monotonous. It comes from combining hum and drum, both of which suggest a constant sound.
Words that go before 'drum'.War: War drums have signaled armies throughout history. They helped coordinate movement across a noisy battlefield.
Words that go before 'drum'.Brake: A brake drum is part of an old style of car brake. Shoes press outward against the inside of a spinning drum.
Words that go before 'drum'.Piano: Piano drum isn't a compound word. Pianos are often classed as percussion, since hammers strike their strings, but the pair doesn't join up.
Words that go before 'drum'.Guitar: Guitar drum isn't a word. Guitar can precede pick, string or solo, but not drum.
Words that go before 'drum'.Flute: Flute drum isn't a phrase. Flute is a wind instrument, so it doesn't pair with drums in a compound.
Words that go before 'drum'.Tea: Tea drum isn't common. You'd say tea cup, tea pot or tea bag.
Words that go before 'drum'.Shoe: Shoe drum isn't a word. Shoe box, shoelace and shoehorn are.
Words that go before 'drum'.Pillow: Pillow drum isn't a word. Pillowcase and pillow fight are.
Words that go before 'drum'.Lamp: Lamp drum isn't a phrase. Lampshade works, but there's no lamp drum.
Words that go before 'drum'.Candle: Candle drum isn't a phrase. Candlestick and candlelight are, but not a candle drum.
Words that go before 'drum'.Book: Book drum isn't a word. Bookmark, bookcase and bookworm are.
Words that go before 'drum'.Cloud: Cloud drum isn't a phrase. Cloudburst is, and thunder is sometimes described as drumming.
Words that go before 'drum'.Sock: Sock drum isn't a word. A sock hop is a dance, though, and drum doesn't fit there.

Music genres that started in the UK.Britpop: The 1990s movement pitted Blur against Oasis in the so-called Battle of Britpop in 1995. Cool Britannia was its cultural moment.
Music genres that started in the UK.Grime: It grew out of East London in the early 2000s, with artists like Dizzee Rascal and Wiley. It has fast, sparse beats at about 140 beats per minute.
Music genres that started in the UK.Drum and bass: It emerged from the UK rave and jungle scene in the 1990s. Its breakbeats are speeded up to around 170 beats per minute.
Music genres that started in the UK.Trip hop: A moody Bristol-born sound from the 1990s, associated with Massive Attack, Portishead and Tricky.
Music genres that started in the UK.Dubstep: It began in the south London clubs around 2000 with heavy sub-bass. Skrillex later popularized an American version.
Music genres that started in the UK.Jungle: A 1990s UK rave offshoot built on fast breakbeats and Jamaican-inspired bass. It later fed into drum and bass.
Music genres that started in the UK.Northern soul: A British scene from the late 1960s, built on rare American soul records played at all-nighters in northern England. Wigan Casino was famous.
Music genres that started in the UK.Madchester: Late 1980s Manchester scene mixing indie rock and dance beats. The Stone Roses and Happy Mondays were central, centered on the Haçienda club.
Music genres that started in the UK.Shoegaze: Named for the band members who stared at their effects pedals. Early 1990s British groups like My Bloody Valentine defined its wall of guitar noise.
Music genres that started in the UK.UK garage: A 1990s London sound with skippy, shuffling beats. Its 2-step style gave rise to later grime and dubstep.
Music genres that started in the UK.Acid jazz: Started in London in the late 1980s, fusing jazz with funk and hip hop. The term was coined by DJ Gilles Peterson and Chris Bangs.
Music genres that started in the UK.Grunge: The sound came from Seattle, Washington, in the late 1980s, with Sub Pop and bands such as Nirvana and Soundgarden.
Music genres that started in the UK.Bluegrass: It was born in the Appalachian US and named after Bill Monroe's Blue Grass Boys. It has Scots-Irish roots, but it's American.
Music genres that started in the UK.Reggae: A Jamaican genre from the late 1960s. Bob Marley took it worldwide.
Music genres that started in the UK.Ska: Jamaican in the 1950s, with offbeat guitar chops. The UK had a second wave called 2 Tone, but ska itself came from Jamaica.
Music genres that started in the UK.K-pop: South Korean pop, with polished idol groups and heavy training. The genre took off in the 1990s.
Music genres that started in the UK.Samba: Brazil's national rhythm grew from Afro-Brazilian roots in Rio and Bahia. It's central to Carnival.
Music genres that started in the UK.Hip hop: Started in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s, with DJ Kool Herc's parties often cited as its birth. It's American in origin.
Music genres that started in the UK.Country: Emerging from Southern Appalachian folk and blues, it was first recorded commercially in the 1920s. It is American.
Music genres that started in the UK.Zydeco: A Louisiana Creole genre featuring accordion and rubboard. It's from French Louisiana, not the UK.
Music genres that started in the UK.Motown: A Detroit label and sound, founded by Berry Gordy in 1959. It's American.
Music genres that started in the UK.Bossa nova: Brazilian, from late 1950s Rio. Its mix of samba and cool jazz was popularized by The Girl from Ipanema.
Music genres that started in the UK.Flamenco: The art form of Andalusia in southern Spain, combining song, guitar and dance. It has Romani roots.
Music genres that started in the UK.House: Named for Chicago's Warehouse club in the early 1980s, it is American. The UK adopted it later.

Bruce Springsteen songs.Born to Run: His 1975 title song and album made him famous, putting him on the covers of Time and Newsweek in the same week.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Born in the USA: Widely mistaken for a flag-waver, it's a bitter song about a struggling Vietnam veteran, though Reagan's 1984 campaign tried to claim it.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Dancing in the Dark: Added late to the 1984 album after his manager asked for a hit. It was written in one night and became his biggest single.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Thunder Road: Its title echoes a 1958 Robert Mitchum film, and the song opens with piano and harmonica before urging Mary to come away.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Glory Days: A 1984 look back at faded high school heroes. Springsteen has said the idea came from bumping into an old friend.
Bruce Springsteen songs.The River: Inspired by his sister and brother-in-law's life when the construction trade collapsed, this 1980 song named his double album.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Hungry Heart: He wrote it for the Ramones, but his manager urged him to keep it, and it became his first top-ten hit in 1980.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Badlands: Opens 1978's Darkness on the Edge of Town with the defiant line 'it ain't no sin to be glad you're alive'.
Bruce Springsteen songs.I'm on Fire: A sparse 1985 song barely over two and a half minutes long, built on a throbbing pulse and a rockabilly shuffle.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Atlantic City: A 1982 song from Nebraska, an album he recorded on a simple four-track cassette recorder at home.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Jack and Diane: Mellencamp's 1982 hit. Another heartland rocker, so it often gets lumped in with Springsteen's catalogue.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Pink Houses: Mellencamp's 1983 song about everyday American life, the kind of thing people mistake for a Springsteen number.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Livin' on a Prayer: Bon Jovi's 1986 anthem. Both are from New Jersey, but this one isn't Springsteen's.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Free Fallin': Tom Petty's 1989 song, co-produced by Jeff Lynne, is known for its soaring chorus and California references.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Runnin' Down a Dream: Another Tom Petty hit, not Springsteen's, though both are heartland-rock figures.
Bruce Springsteen songs.American Pie: Don McLean's 1971 epic about the day the music died, the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Hotel California: The Eagles' 1976 classic. California, not New Jersey, so it's a trap for heartland-rock fans.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Sweet Home Alabama: Lynyrd Skynyrd's 1974 reply to Neil Young's songs criticising the South, with a famous guitar intro.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Piano Man: Billy Joel's 1973 song. Springsteen and Joel are both New York area icons, but this is Joel's.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Born to Be Wild: Steppenwolf's 1968 anthem has the line 'heavy metal thunder', one of the first uses of the term in a rock lyric.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Born This Way: Lady Gaga's 2011 anthem shares the word 'Born' with Springsteen titles but belongs to pop, not heartland rock.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Born Slippy: Underworld's 1996 rave anthem, made famous by the film Trainspotting. Another 'Born' title that isn't Springsteen's.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Like a Rolling Stone: Bob Dylan's 1965 six-minute landmark, which changed pop by ignoring the three-minute limit.
Bruce Springsteen songs.Small Town: Mellencamp's 1985 hit about a small-town upbringing. Heartland rock, but not Springsteen's.

U2 songs.With or Without You: The Joshua Tree's biggest hit; the Edge's sustain device gives its ringing riff an endless shimmer, and it became U2's first US number one.
U2 songs.One: Written during tense Berlin sessions for Achtung Baby in 1991; Bono sings of unity, though the lyrics are about quarrels and forgiveness.
U2 songs.Beautiful Day: Won Record of the Year at the 2001 Grammys, and U2 won it again the next year with Walk On, a rare back-to-back feat.
U2 songs.Sunday Bloody Sunday: Written about the 1972 Bloody Sunday shootings in Derry; Larry Mullen's military snare drum opens it, and Bono waves a white flag at live shows.
U2 songs.Pride: Officially Pride (In the Name of Love), about Martin Luther King; Bono famously sings that he was shot in the early morning, though it was evening.
U2 songs.Vertigo: The 2004 single opens with Bono counting Uno, dos, tres, catorce; it fronted an iPod ad that put U2 in many ears.
U2 songs.Elevation: The song for Tomb Raider's film soundtrack, released in 2000; Bono sings of wanting to be lifted up, over a pulsing groove.
U2 songs.Mysterious Ways: The wah-wah guitar from The Edge drives this Achtung Baby single, and a belly-dancing video helped make it a hit.
U2 songs.Desire: From Rattle and Hum (1988), built on a Bo Diddley beat; it gave U2 their first UK number one.
U2 songs.New Year's Day: Inspired by Poland's Solidarity movement, though many think it is about a holiday; Adam Clayton's bass line opens it.
U2 songs.Stuck in a Moment: The full title is Stuck in a Moment You Can't Get Out Of, reportedly written to Michael Hutchence after his death.
U2 songs.Zombie: The Cranberries, 1994. Their song of anger at the IRA's Warrington bombing is from Ireland, like U2, but a different band.
U2 songs.Linger: Another Cranberries hit, from the same Limerick group, not U2.
U2 songs.Dreams: Another Cranberries song from Everybody Else Is Doing It, a mellow Irish band's hit; not U2.
U2 songs.Yellow: Coldplay, 2000, from a British band often compared to U2 for big, anthemic sound.
U2 songs.Clocks: Coldplay, 2002, with its famous piano riff; U2-like, but it isn't theirs.
U2 songs.Fix You: Coldplay, 2005, a ballad U2 would have been proud to write, but it isn't theirs.
U2 songs.Viva la Vida: Coldplay, 2008, named after a Frida Kahlo painting; it's another band entirely.
U2 songs.Roxanne: The Police, 1978; Sting's story of a streetwalker is a different British band's song.
U2 songs.Message in a Bottle: The Police, 1979; Sting's song about a lonely man sending an SOS is not U2.
U2 songs.Mr. Brightside: The Killers, 2003. An American band's jealousy song, not an Irish one.
U2 songs.Chasing Cars: Snow Patrol, 2006. A mellow Northern Irish band's hit, like U2, from Ireland, but another group.
U2 songs.Losing My Religion: R.E.M., 1991, the Georgia band's biggest hit; U2's friends, but not their song.
U2 songs.Everybody Hurts: R.E.M., 1992, a ballad meant to reach young people who feel hopeless; not U2.

Instrument names that are also verbs.Drum: Drumming is among humanity's oldest music; as a verb, you drum up business or drum something into someone's head.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Harp: To harp on is to dwell on one subject, a figure that comes from a harpist plucking the same string repeatedly.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Fiddle: To fiddle means to fidget or to tamper with, and a fiddle is exactly the same instrument as a violin.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Trumpet: To trumpet means to announce loudly, and elephants also trumpet when excited.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Pipe: To pipe up means to speak out suddenly; pipe is also a verb for decorating a cake with icing.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Whistle: To whistle-blow comes from referees and police halting action with a whistle; the verb whistle itself is as old as speech.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Rattle: To rattle someone is to unsettle them, and rattlesnakes are named for the noise-making segments on their tails.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Chime: To chime in is to add a remark to a conversation, an idea borrowed from bells ringing together.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Horn: To horn in means to intrude, a phrase from American slang; animal horns are made of keratin, like fingernails.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Piano: A noun only: Bartolomeo Cristofori invented the piano in Florence around 1700, and its name is short for pianoforte, soft-loud.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Violin: Violin is only a noun; the instrument is also called a fiddle, which can be a verb.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Cello: Short for violoncello, meaning little big viola; it's strictly a noun, and no one cellos.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Tuba: From a Latin word for trumpet; the tuba is a noun, though a tuba's coiled tubing can reach around 18 feet.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Oboe: The name comes from French hautbois, high wood; the oboe is a noun with no verb sense.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Mandolin: A small Italian lute-like instrument; no verb meaning, despite how nicely it strums.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Guitar: Nobody guitars; the word is a noun only, with roots in an ancient Greek stringed instrument, the kithara.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Ukulele: Hawaiian for jumping flea, named for the way the player's fingers dance; it's not a verb.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Clarinet: The instrument Mozart wrote a famous concerto for; the clarinet has no verb sense.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Bassoon: Its name comes from Italian fagotto, a bundle of sticks, and it has no verb sense.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Viola: Slightly larger than a violin; viola is also a flower, but neither is a verb.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Sitar: Ravi Shankar made the sitar famous in the West; its name comes from a Persian word meaning three strings.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Harmonica: Also known as a mouth organ, the harmonica is strictly a noun.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Xylophone: The word comes from Greek for wood sound; xylophone has no verb sense.
Instrument names that are also verbs.Accordion: Invented in Vienna in 1829; no one accordions, so this is a noun only.

Basketball legends.Shaquille O'Neal: The 7-foot-1 center won four NBA titles, three of them in a row with the Lakers alongside Kobe Bryant.
Basketball legends.Stephen Curry: His deep three-pointers changed how the game is played, and he holds the NBA record for career threes.
Basketball legends.Magic Johnson: The 6-foot-9 point guard won five titles with the Lakers and shocked the world by announcing he was HIV positive in 1991.
Basketball legends.Larry Bird: A Celtics forward who won three straight MVP awards in the mid-1980s, he fueled the classic rivalry with Magic Johnson.
Basketball legends.Kareem Abdul-Jabbar: He held the NBA career scoring record for almost four decades, using his famous skyhook shot; he was born Lew Alcindor.
Basketball legends.Kevin Durant: A 6-foot-10 forward with guard-like shooting, he won back-to-back Finals MVP awards with the Warriors in 2017 and 2018.
Basketball legends.Tim Duncan: Nicknamed 'The Big Fundamental', he won five titles over 19 seasons, all with the San Antonio Spurs.
Basketball legends.Dirk Nowitzki: The German star led Dallas to the 2011 title and made the one-legged fadeaway his signature shot.
Basketball legends.Tom Brady: A football quarterback with seven Super Bowl rings, not a basketball player, though baseball's Expos once drafted him.
Basketball legends.Peyton Manning: The QB won five NFL MVP awards, a record, and two Super Bowls; his brother Eli also won two Super Bowls.
Basketball legends.Derek Jeter: The Yankees shortstop won five World Series and collected 3,465 hits, so his sport is baseball.
Basketball legends.Babe Ruth: Baseball's Ruth began as a pitcher, hit 60 homers in 1927, and has no link to the NBA.
Basketball legends.Wayne Gretzky: Hockey's 'The Great One' wore 99, a number retired league-wide, and he never played basketball.
Basketball legends.Lionel Messi: A soccer superstar with a record eight Ballon d'Or awards; his sport is football, played with the feet.

Basketball legends.Tiger Woods: A golfer with 15 major titles, famous for his red Sunday shirts, not a basketball player.
Basketball legends.Roger Federer: A tennis star with 20 Grand Slam singles titles and a famously smooth one-handed backhand.
Basketball legends.Usain Bolt: The sprinter holds the 100m and 200m world records, and he's famous for his lightning-bolt pose, not a jump shot.
Basketball legends.Joe Montana: The 49ers quarterback won four Super Bowls and never threw an interception in any of them.
Basketball legends.Mike Tyson: The boxer became the youngest heavyweight champion ever, aged 20, in 1986; his sport is boxing.
Basketball legends.Sidney Crosby: The Penguins captain scored the golden goal at the 2010 Vancouver Olympics, so his sport is hockey.

Toys designed to spin.Spinning top: Spinning tops date back thousands of years; examples survive from ancient Ur. A top stays upright because spin angular momentum resists tipping.
Toys designed to spin.Yo-yo: The word may come from Filipino, and in the 1920s Pedro Flores began mass-producing yo-yos in California. One was even taken aboard a space shuttle.
Toys designed to spin.Fidget spinner: Spinners boomed in 2017, yet the toy's patent was filed in the 1990s by Catherine Hettinger, who never made money from it.
Toys designed to spin.Beyblade: Launched in Japan in 1999, these battling tops grew into a huge franchise with anime and manga. Their name blends 'bey' (to spin) and 'blade'.
Toys designed to spin.Dreidel: This four-sided top is spun at Hanukkah, each side bearing a Hebrew letter that stands for 'A great miracle happened there'.
Toys designed to spin.Pinwheel: A pinwheel spins because wind pushes the angled blades. In Japan the similar kazaguruma is a traditional toy often left at memorial sites.
Toys designed to spin.Gyroscope: A spinning gyroscope resists changes to its orientation, which is why the principle guides aircraft, ships and spacecraft in navigation systems.
Toys designed to spin.Whirligig: The name covers spinning toys and wind-driven garden ornaments alike. Folk whirligigs often show little figures that flap their arms in the breeze.
Toys designed to spin.Diabolo: A diabolo is an hourglass-shaped spool whipped along a string between two sticks, and it can be tossed high into the air. It is a staple of circus acts.
Toys designed to spin.Slinky: Slinky was invented by accident in 1943 when a naval engineer saw a tension spring fall and step across a shelf. It walks, but it does not spin.
Toys designed to spin.Silly Putty: Silly Putty came from failed attempts to make synthetic rubber in WWII. It bounces, stretches and even copies newsprint, but it doesn't spin.
Toys designed to spin.Play-Doh: Play-Doh began life as a wallpaper cleaner before becoming a modeling compound in the 1950s. It is for squishing, not spinning.
Toys designed to spin.Lego: The name comes from the Danish 'leg godt', meaning 'play well'. Bricks from the 1950s still fit with ones made today, but nothing spins.
Toys designed to spin.Teddy bear: Teddy bears are named for President Theodore Roosevelt, who famously refused to shoot a tied-up bear on a 1902 hunt. They're cuddled, not spun.
Toys designed to spin.Kite: Kites fly rather than spin. They were invented in China over 2,000 years ago and were once used to measure distances and send signals.
Toys designed to spin.Pogo stick: A pogo stick bounces on a spring; no spinning needed. Its name probably comes from its inventors' initials or surname.
Toys designed to spin.Rubber duck: Rubber ducks became a bath icon, and in 1992 a shipping spill sent thousands drifting, helping oceanographers study currents.
Toys designed to spin.Slime: Slime is a non-Newtonian goo, usually made from glue and borax or similar activators. It stretches and oozes, but it doesn't spin.
Toys designed to spin.Tamagotchi: This 1996 Japanese egg-shaped pet had to be fed and cleaned on a tiny screen. It demanded attention, not rotation.
Toys designed to spin.Magic 8 Ball: This fortune-telling toy has a floating die inside with 20 answers, 10 of them affirmative. You shake it rather than spin it.
Toys designed to spin.Mr. Potato Head: Mr. Potato Head first shipped in 1952 as plastic parts to stick into a real potato, and it was the first toy advertised on TV.
Toys designed to spin.Barbie: Barbie debuted in 1959 and is named after Barbara, the daughter of creator Ruth Handler. She poses and strikes outfits rather than spinning.
Toys designed to spin.Water gun: Water guns squirt with a pump or pressure rather than spin. The Super Soaker from the 1990s was invented by NASA engineer Lonnie Johnson.
Toys designed to spin.Bubble wand: A wand dips into soapy water and you blow a bubble. The bubble may spin as it floats, but the wand itself isn't designed to.

Solitaire (patience) card games.Klondike: Klondike is what most people call plain solitaire. It's named for the Yukon gold rush region, and a random deal is winnable roughly 80 percent of the time.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Spider: Spider uses two decks and builds descending sequences within a suit. It's one of the hardest common solitaire games.
Solitaire (patience) card games.FreeCell: FreeCell has four open cells and nearly every deal is solvable; only one of the first 32,000 numbered deals can't be won.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Pyramid: Pyramid asks players to pair cards adding up to 13, working through a stack of cards arranged in a pyramid.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Golf: Here, golf is a solitaire game where cards are played to a foundation in sequence, up or down one rank, much like a round with par.
Solitaire (patience) card games.TriPeaks: TriPeaks lays three overlapping peaks of cards, and you clear them by chaining cards one rank higher or lower.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Yukon: Yukon resembles Klondike, but you can move any face-up card with the cards on top, even if they aren't in sequence.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Canfield: Canfield is said to be named for a casino owner who sold decks to players and paid them for each card played to the foundation.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Forty Thieves: Forty Thieves is a famously hard solitaire with two decks, and wins are rare, which is why it's also called Napoleon at St Helena.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Accordion: Accordion deals cards in a single line and you pile them onto earlier cards of matching suit or value. It's very short but hard to win.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Scorpion: Scorpion is a solitaire where you can move any card, together with those on top, which makes it permissive.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Poker: Poker is played against other players, so it can't be solitaire; the game requires bluffing opponents.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Rummy: Rummy needs two or more players making sets and runs. Some variants, like gin rummy, are played by two.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Bridge: Bridge is a four-player partnership game and a competitive mind sport, not solitaire.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Hearts: Hearts needs several players avoiding penalty cards. Microsoft included it in Windows to teach mouse use, alongside Solitaire.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Go Fish: Go Fish is a children's game of asking others for matching ranks, so it needs at least two players.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Snap: Snap is a quick children's game: players shout when two matching cards appear, and you need an opponent.
Solitaire (patience) card games.War: War is a purely luck-based two-player game, with no decisions, so it's the opposite of a solo game.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Blackjack: Blackjack pits the player against a dealer, and the house edge is small if you follow basic strategy. Not a solitaire.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Canasta: Canasta, meaning basket in Spanish, emerged in Uruguay in the 1930s and is played in partnerships.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Euchre: Euchre is a trick-taking game for four players, popular in the Midwest, and the word is thought to be Germanic.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Cribbage: Cribbage is scored on a peg board, and it's played by two to four people. The inventor is said to be Sir John Suckling.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Old Maid: Old Maid is played by drawing from neighbors and avoiding being left with the odd queen, so you need others.
Solitaire (patience) card games.Spades: Spades is a four-player partnership trick-taking game, popular in the US since the 1930s.

Parts of a medieval castle.Moat: A ditch around the walls, often filled with water, which kept attackers from tunneling under or rolling siege towers close.
Parts of a medieval castle.Drawbridge: A bridge across the moat that could be raised to block the gate. Raising it quickly could stop an attack cold.
Parts of a medieval castle.Keep: The strongest tower, the last refuge when outer walls fell. It often housed the lord's family and stored supplies.
Parts of a medieval castle.Portcullis: A heavy gate of wood or iron, lowered vertically to seal an entrance. Murder holes above allowed defenders to drop things on intruders.
Parts of a medieval castle.Battlements: The notched parapet along the wall top. The raised parts, merlons, shielded archers while gaps let them shoot.
Parts of a medieval castle.Turret: A small tower built on the corner of a wall or larger tower. It offered a lookout and extra firing positions.
Parts of a medieval castle.Gatehouse: A fortified building around the entrance. It was the castle's weakest point, so builders packed it with defenses.
Parts of a medieval castle.Bailey: The enclosed courtyard inside the walls. It held stables, workshops and kitchens, and in motte-and-bailey castles it sat below the hill.
Parts of a medieval castle.Arrow slit: A narrow window that let archers shoot while exposing little of themselves. The thin shape was easy to defend and tough to hit.
Parts of a medieval castle.Great hall: The main room for feasting, meetings and sometimes sleeping. Nobles hosted banquets here, with open hearths at the center.
Parts of a medieval castle.Dungeon: The word comes from donjon, another term for the keep. Dungeons were often storage cellars and not prisons.
Parts of a medieval castle.Curtain wall: The thick outer wall linking towers. Some walls were over ten feet thick, built to withstand siege engines.
Parts of a medieval castle.Skyscraper: A modern high-rise. The first, the Home Insurance Building in Chicago, rose in 1885, centuries after castle building.
Parts of a medieval castle.Elevator: A modern lift for buildings. Safety elevators came with Otis in the 1850s, long after castles were built.
Parts of a medieval castle.Garage: A shelter for cars, a modern invention. Castles had stables for horses instead, often right inside the bailey.
Parts of a medieval castle.Escalator: A moving stair, from the late 1800s. Castles had narrow spiral stairs, often turning clockwise to disadvantage attackers.
Parts of a medieval castle.Driveway: A path for cars. Medieval castles had approach roads, but they were not built for vehicles.
Parts of a medieval castle.Carport: A roofed shelter for cars, a 20th century invention. Medieval castles had stables for horses, not parking spots.
Parts of a medieval castle.Sunroom: A glassed-in room for sunlight. Large glass windows were rare and costly in the Middle Ages.
Parts of a medieval castle.Hot tub: A modern heated bath for leisure. Medieval castles had basic bathing and garderobes, which were toilets.
Parts of a medieval castle.Doorbell: An electric doorbell dates to the 1800s. Castle visitors blew a horn or shouted at the gate.
Parts of a medieval castle.Swimming pool: A modern leisure pool. Castles had a moat for defense, and nobody swam in it for fun, given what went into it.
Parts of a medieval castle.Solar panel: Photovoltaic panels date from the 1950s. The medieval castle did have a solar, but that was a private upstairs room.
Parts of a medieval castle.Mailbox: A modern postal box. In medieval times, letters were carried by messengers on horseback, and most people couldn't read anyway.

Renaissance figures.Leonardo da Vinci: Painter, engineer and anatomist who filled thousands of notebook pages, often in mirror writing. He left only about 15 finished paintings.
Renaissance figures.Michelangelo: Sculpted the David at 26, and painted the Sistine ceiling mostly standing, not lying down. He considered himself a sculptor first.
Renaissance figures.Raphael: Died at 37 on his birthday, according to Vasari. His School of Athens fresco in the Vatican places Leonardo's face on Plato.
Renaissance figures.Botticelli: The Birth of Venus painter, who fell out of fashion after his death and was rediscovered in the 19th century. He is now among the Renaissance's best known.
Renaissance figures.Machiavelli: A Florentine diplomat whose book The Prince, written in 1513, advised rulers to be feared as well as loved. His name gave us "Machiavellian".
Renaissance figures.Copernicus: Polish astronomer who put the Sun at the centre of the cosmos in a book published in 1543, the year he died. He allegedly saw a first copy on his deathbed.
Renaissance figures.Erasmus: Dutch scholar, "the prince of the humanists", who produced the first printed Greek New Testament in 1516. He wrote In Praise of Folly.
Renaissance figures.Titian: Venetian master of colour who painted for kings and popes and worked into his late 80s. His warm reds became so famous that they were named "Titian red".
Renaissance figures.Brunelleschi: The architect of Florence Cathedral's enormous dome, which he built without wooden scaffolding using a herringbone brick pattern. He also helped develop linear perspective.
Renaissance figures.Donatello: Florentine sculptor whose bronze David (about 1440) was the first freestanding nude statue since antiquity. The Ninja Turtle bears his name.
Renaissance figures.Plato: An ancient Greek philosopher, not Renaissance. Renaissance thinkers revived his ideas, but he lived around 400 BC.
Renaissance figures.Julius Caesar: A Roman general murdered in 44 BC, over 1,400 years before the Renaissance. Renaissance artists loved Roman themes, but he was ancient.
Renaissance figures.Charlemagne: The Frankish emperor crowned in AD 800. He belongs to the early Middle Ages, long before the Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Napoleon: French emperor who rose after the French Revolution, around 1800, three centuries after the Renaissance peaked.
Renaissance figures.Isaac Newton: A figure of the Scientific Revolution, who published his laws of motion in 1687. He came a good while after the Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Beethoven: German composer, working around 1800. A figure of the Classical and Romantic eras, not the Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Mozart: A Classical composer who lived 1756 to 1791. He came about two centuries after the Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Charles Darwin: The Victorian naturalist behind On the Origin of Species, published in 1859. He lived centuries after the Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Einstein: 20th-century physicist who proposed relativity in 1905 and 1915, four centuries after the Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Van Gogh: A Dutch Post-Impressionist who painted in the 1880s. He sold very few paintings in life, and lived 350 years too late for the Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Picasso: A 20th-century Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism. He is modern, not Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Cleopatra: The last active pharaoh of Egypt, who died in 30 BC, roughly 1,500 years before the Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Socrates: The Athenian philosopher who died in 399 BC after being sentenced to drink hemlock. He is classical, not Renaissance.
Renaissance figures.Monet: The Impressionist behind Water Lilies, who lived from 1840 to 1926. He belongs to the 19th century.

Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Walter Raleigh: He sponsored the lost colony of Roanoke, and was later imprisoned in the Tower.

Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.John Dee: The Queen's mathematician and astrologer, with one of the biggest libraries in England.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Edmund Spenser: His epic The Faerie Queene flatters Elizabeth as its hidden heroine, and he was buried near Chaucer.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Ben Jonson: A playwright and Shakespeare's friendly rival. He once escaped hanging for killing an actor by claiming clergy privilege.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Philip Sidney: A poet and soldier who died in 1586 from a wound at Zutphen, and was a national hero.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.William Cecil: As Lord Burghley, he was the queen's chief minister for nearly 40 years and her most trusted adviser.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Henry VIII: Elizabeth's father died in 1547, when she was 13, so he missed her reign entirely.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Isaac Newton: Born in 1642, nearly 40 years after Elizabeth died, he belongs to the next century of English science.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Chaucer: He died in 1400, over 150 years before Elizabeth took the throne, so he belongs to the medieval world.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Charles Dickens: A Victorian novelist of the 1800s, nearly 300 years after Elizabeth's reign had ended.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Samuel Pepys: His famous diary covers the 1660s, including the Great Fire of London, 60 years after Elizabeth died.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Lord Byron: The Romantic poet lived from 1788 to 1824, and died in Greece fighting for its independence, long after.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Jane Austen: She wrote in the early 1800s, about two centuries after Elizabeth I died.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Thomas Becket: The archbishop was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170, four centuries earlier.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.King Arthur: A legendary king, said to have lived some 1,000 years before Elizabeth.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Charles Darwin: A Victorian naturalist born in 1809, about two centuries after Elizabeth's day, who sailed on HMS Beagle.
Famous people of Elizabeth I's England.Christopher Wren: Born in 1632, he rebuilt London after the Great Fire of 1666, long after Elizabeth.
